why: Theorem 1 (SAT/tautology-deciding is P-reducible-complete for polynomial-time-nondeterministic decidability), its A(w) proof construction, Theorem 2 (the first family of problems sharing one polynomial degree of difficulty), the P-reducibility and deg(S) definitions, and Cook's own statement of the open P-vs-NP-equivalent conjecture

title: George Logemann, Donald Loveland, "A machine program for theorem-proving", CACM 5(7):394-397

title: "Clustering at the Phase Transition", AAAI-97
why: unary prime implicates (backbone literals); a large subclass of random 3-SAT instances at the phase transition has roughly 85-95% of variables in UPIs, and their models cluster

title: John Slaney, Sylvie Thiébaux, Toby Walsh, "Backbones and Backdoors in Satisfiability", AAAI 2005, 1368-1373
why: backbone = literals true in every satisfying assignment; computing it is NP-hard and NP-easy, polynomial iff P=NP; the backbone is hard even to approximate to within a fixed fraction unless P=NP; backbones and backdoors overlap little

title: "The Complexity of Enumeration and Reliability Problems", SIAM J. Comput. 8(3):410-421

title: Riccardo Zecchina, Scott Kirkpatrick, Bart Selman, Lidror Troyansky, "Determining computational complexity from characteristic 'phase transitions'", Nature 400:133-137

title: "Pragmatic Presuppositions", in Semantics and Philosophy (Munitz & Unger, eds.), NYU Press; repr. in Context and Content, OUP 1999
why: Presupposition is a speaker attitude (taking P for granted and assuming the audience recognises it); the common ground is modelled as a context set of possible worlds that accepted utterances shrink.

title: "Presuppositions of Compound Sentences", Linguistic Inquiry 4(2):169-193
why: The plugs/holes/filters typology of presupposition projection: negation and interrogative environments are holes, so a presupposition survives being questioned or denied.

title: "Scorekeeping in a Language Game", Journal of Philosophical Logic 8:339-359
why: The rule of accommodation for presupposition: if what is said requires P to be acceptable and P is not presupposed just before, P comes into existence at that moment.

title: "Eyewitness testimony: The influence of the wording of a question", Bulletin of the Psychonomic Society 5(1):86-88
why: Questions with a definite article ("the broken headlight") produced fewer uncertain responses and more recognition of events that never occurred than the indefinite-article version. — verifier 2026-09-08: does NOT support the cited claim

title: Phu Mon Htut, Samuel R. Bowman, Jackson Petty, "(QA)^2: Question Answering with Questionable Assumptions", ACL 2023 (Long Papers), pp. 8466-8487
why: Naturally occurring search queries often carry false or unverifiable assumptions; current models struggle to detect them and answer as if the assumption held.

title: "Logic and Conversation", in Syntax and Semantics 3: Speech Acts (Cole & Morgan, eds.), Academic Press (repr. Brill, ISBN 9789004368576), pp. 41-58 [book]
why: The Cooperative Principle and the maxims of Quantity, Quality, Relation and Manner; what a cooperative answer conveys beyond what it says is defeasible implicature.

title: "Questions", Australasian Journal of Philosophy 36(3):159–168
why: The three postulates: an answer is a statement; knowing a question's meaning is knowing what counts as an answer to it; the possible answers exhaust the possibilities. Also the 'In which continent is Honolulu?' false-presupposition example.

title: The Logic of Questions and Answers, Yale University Press
authors: Nuel D. Belnap Jr. & Thomas B. Steel Jr.
why: A question presupposes a statement iff the truth of that statement is a logically necessary condition for the question's having a true answer (p. 5); on presupposition failure the cooperative reply is a corrective, not a direct answer.

title: Studies on the Semantics of Questions and the Pragmatics of Answers, PhD thesis, University of Amsterdam
why: Partition semantics: a question denotes at each world the true exhaustive answer there, so the question is a partition of logical space and worlds within a cell are indistinguishable by it.

title: Jeroen Groenendijk & Floris Roelofsen, Inquisitive Semantics, Oxford University Press
why: Question meaning as a downward-closed set of resolving propositions, replacing the partition to cover conditional, alternative and mention-some questions — cited in Limits as the failure case of partition theory.

title: B. G. & Strauss, A. L., The Discovery of Grounded Theory: Strategies for Qualitative Research. Aldine.
why: Definition of theoretical sampling as joint collection/coding/analysis deciding what data to collect next, and of theoretical saturation as the point where no further properties of a category emerge.

title: G., Bunce, A. & Johnson, L., 'How Many Interviews Are Enough? An Experiment with Data Saturation and Variability', Field Methods 18(1):59-82
why: In 60 interviews across two West African countries, saturation occurred within the first 12 interviews, with metatheme basics present by 6.

title: M. M., Kaiser, B. N. & Marconi, V. C., 'Code Saturation Versus Meaning Saturation: How Many Interviews Are Enough?', Qualitative Health Research 27(4):591-608
why: Code saturation reached at 9 interviews, meaning saturation at 16-24 on the same dataset; 'heard it all' vs 'understand it all'.

title: G., Namey, E. & Chen, M., 'A simple method to assess and report thematic saturation in qualitative research', PLOS ONE 15(5):e0232076
why: Operational saturation rule with base size, run length and new information threshold; recommended base 4, run 2-3, threshold <=5% or 0%; datasets crossed <=5% at 6+2 and 8-9+2 interviews; validated by bootstrapping completed datasets.

title: M. & Kaiser, B. N., 'Sample sizes for saturation in qualitative research: A systematic review of empirical tests', Social Science & Medicine 292:114523
why: Systematic review of 23 empirical tests: saturation at 9-17 interviews or 4-8 focus groups for homogeneous populations with narrow aims; larger samples for broader aims or theoretical saturation.

title: B. et al., 'Saturation in qualitative research: exploring its conceptualization and operationalization', Quality & Quantity 52:1893-1907
why: Saturation names four distinct models differing in whether theory, codes, data or meaning is what saturates. — verifier 2026-09-08: does NOT support the cited claim

title: K., Siersma, V. D. & Guassora, A. D., 'Sample Size in Qualitative Interview Studies: Guided by Information Power', Qualitative Health Research 26(13):1753-1760
why: Information power as a non-countable alternative to saturation, depending on study aim, sample specificity, use of established theory, quality of dialogue, and analysis strategy.

title: A New Approach to the Logical Theory of Interrogatives, Uppsala (Filosofiska Föreningen)
why: The imperative-epistemic theory of questions: to ask a question is to issue an imperative requiring the addressee to bring it about that the speaker knows the answer. Cited jointly with Hintikka by SEP 'Questions' §4.1; primary text not seen.

title: The Semantics of Questions and the Questions of Semantics, Acta Philosophica Fennica 28, North-Holland
why: The desideratum of a question: 'Who is b?' is a request to bring it about that the asker knows who b is, formalised ∃x K(b = x); the study of questions reduces to the study of their desiderata.

title: 'On sense, reference, and the objects of knowledge' and 'Reasoning about knowledge in philosophy: the paradigm of epistemic logic', in The Logic of Epistemology and the Epistemology of Logic: Selected Essays, Kluwer/Springer
why: The conclusiveness condition: K M(a,b) does not entail ∃x K M(x,b) — the asker must also know who a is, ∃x K(a = x); and the world-line / identification-scheme machinery (perspectival vs public identification) on which the condition depends.

title: Socratic Epistemology: Explorations of Knowledge-Seeking by Questioning, Cambridge University Press
why: The interrogative model of inquiry: a principal question is answered through a chain of smaller operative questions put to a source of information, so knowledge-seeking is interrogation.

title: 'Beyond knowing that: a new generation of epistemic logics', arXiv:1605.01995 (in Jaakko Hintikka on Knowledge and Game-Theoretical Semantics, Springer)
why: §2.1 states the desideratum, the ∃xKM(x,b) formalisation, the conclusiveness condition and its functional generalisation ∃f K∀x(f(x)=g(x)) (Hintikka 1996, 1999); records that it is debatable how pervasive the requirement is; and notes that quantified epistemic logics are frequently undecidable.

title: T. S., Budescu, D. V., Rapoport, A., Zwick, R., & Forsyth, B. — Measuring the vague meanings of probability terms. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General 115(4), 348–365
why: Vague meanings of probability terms are measurable as membership functions over [0,1] by pair comparison; individual differences are large but stable, and the derived functions predict independent judgments.

title: D. V., & Wallsten, T. S. — Consistency in interpretation of probabilistic phrases. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 36, 391–405
why: Within-subject variability in mapping phrases to numbers is considerably smaller than between-subject variability.

title: S. — Words of Estimative Probability. Studies in Intelligence 8(4)
why: Operational failure of estimative language: the same word ('probable') read as roughly 75% by some readers and 30% by others; a fixed lexicon proposed as the remedy.

title: D. V., Broomell, S., & Por, H.-H. — Improving communication of uncertainty in the reports of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Psychological Science 20(3), 299–308
why: Readers' numeric interpretations of IPCC probability terms departed from the published guidelines even when the guidelines were available to them.

title: D. V., Por, H.-H., & Broomell, S. B. — Effective communication of uncertainty in the IPCC reports. Climatic Change 113, 181–200
why: The public misinterprets probabilistic statements regressively; a dual verbal–numerical scale increases differentiation, cross-reader consistency and consistency with the guidelines, independent of ideology; interpretation also depends on context (base rate, severity).

title: I., & Cohen, B. L. — Verbal versus numerical probabilities: efficiency, biases, and the preference paradox. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 45(1), 1–18
why: Communication mode preference paradox: senders convey probabilities verbally while receivers prefer to receive them numerically.

title: K. H., & Brun, W. — The directionality of verbal probability expressions: effects on decisions, predictions, and probabilistic reasoning. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 80(2), 155–190
why: Positive and negative phrases judged to carry the same numeric probability produce opposite decisions and predictions.

title: T. M., & Budescu, D. V. — You say 'probable' and I say 'likely': improving interpersonal communication with verbal probability phrases. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied 10(1), 25–41
why: Communication improves by translating a phrase through the sender's own lexicon into the receiver's, rather than through a shared standard.

title: Z., Shen, K., & Kejriwal, M. — An Evaluation of Estimative Uncertainty in Large Language Models. arXiv:2405.15185
why: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 align with human numeric interpretations for some words of estimative probability but not others, with divergence under Chinese-language and gendered-role contexts.

title: E. et al. — Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations (arXiv 2212.09251; ACL Findings 2023)
why: Sycophancy — repeating back a dialog user's preferred answer — increases with model size and with the number of RLHF steps; an early inverse-scaling result inside RLHF.

title: M., Tong, M., Korbak, T., Duvenaud, D., Askell, A., Bowman, S. R. et al. — Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models (arXiv 2310.13548; ICLR 2024)
why: Sycophancy across five deployed assistants is driven in part by human preference judgments: a response matching the user's view is more likely to be preferred, humans and preference models pick convincingly-written sycophantic responses over correct ones a non-negligible fraction of the time, and optimising against a PM sometimes sacrifices truthfulness.

title: K., Hwang, J. D., Ren, X., & Sap, M. — Relying on the Unreliable: The Impact of Language Models' Reluctance to Express Uncertainty (arXiv 2401.06730; ACL 2024)
why: Human preference datasets are biased against weakeners (8% less often chosen than strengtheners, 9% less than plain text); the OpenAssistant deberta-v3-large-v2 reward model scores plain statements 4.03, strengtheners 0.82, weakeners -1.86 on 183 QA pairs; RLHF'd models emit more strengtheners than weakeners while base/SFT models do the reverse.

title: M. J. Q., Knox, W. B., & Choi, E. — Modeling Future Conversation Turns to Teach LLMs to Ask Clarifying Questions (arXiv 2410.13788; ICLR 2025)
why: Preference labels are assigned on prior contexts only, so a clarifying question earns no credit for the turn it enables; labelling by simulated future turns gives +5 F1 across interpretations and +3 accuracy on ask-versus-answer.

title: OpenAI — Expanding on what we missed with sycophancy
authors: OpenAI — Expanding on what we missed with sycophancy
why: The 25 April 2025 GPT-4o update was rolled back on 28 April; OpenAI attributed it in part to added user thumbs-up/down reward signals that 'weakened the influence of our primary reward signal, which had been holding sycophancy in check.'

title: V. & Clarke, V., 'To saturate or not to saturate? Questioning data saturation as a useful concept for thematic analysis and sample-size rationales', Qualitative Research in Sport, Exercise and Health 13(2):201-216, doi:10.1080/2159676X.2019.1704846
why: Information redundancy presupposes meaning residing in the data; under reflexive thematic analysis interpretation never exhausts, so no novelty count can terminate — and information power is proposed instead.

title: A. van Lamsweerde, S. Fickas, "Goal-directed requirements acquisition", Science of Computer Programming 20(1-2):3-50, 1993
why: KAOS: requirements acquired as an AND/OR graph of goals with agents to be assigned and alternatives to be negotiated.

title: "Goal-Oriented Requirements Engineering: A Guided Tour", Proc. RE'01, 5th IEEE Int. Symp. on Requirements Engineering, Toronto, 2001, pp. 249-263
why: Completeness criterion R,As,D |= g and R,As,D |/= false; pertinence (a requirement is pertinent iff its specification is used in the proof of at least one goal, after Yue 1987); requirement vs assumption by single-agent responsibility; HOW/WHY questions as refinement and abstraction operators; the '2-button' optional formal layer; alternative-refinement and agent-assignment selection stated as an open problem (Sec. 5.6).

title: A. van Lamsweerde, "Agent-Based Tactics for Goal-Oriented Requirements Elaboration", Proc. ICSE 2002, pp. 83-93
why: Refine goals until assignable to single agents; assign only if the agent can realize the goal — realizability requires monitorability of antecedent variables and controllability of consequent variables; refinement tactics when it fails.

title: "Towards Modelling and Reasoning Support for Early-Phase Requirements Engineering", Proc. 3rd IEEE Int. Symp. on Requirements Engineering (RE'97), pp. 226-235
why: i* models intentional dependencies among actors (Strategic Dependency / Strategic Rationale), a different object from KAOS refinement-with-entailment; hence 'goal-oriented RE' names a family broader than the KAOS goal graph.

title: Yifan Luo, Huadong Wang, Xingyi Cheng, Zhiyuan Liu, Maosong Sun, "Won't Get Fooled Again: Answering Questions with False Premises", ACL 2023 (Long Papers)
why: FalseQA: 2,365 human-written false-premise questions; fine-tuning on ~256 examples is enough for PLMs to discriminate them, so the rebutting knowledge is present but not the default behaviour.

title: Inês Lynce, Joao Marques-Silva, "Algorithms for computing backbones of propositional formulae", AI Communications 28(2):161-177
why: Backbone as the set of necessary assignments; the literature's variant names for the same object (inadmissible/necessary variables, bound literals, fixed assignments, units, frozen variables), §1; large instances from practical applications often have backbones close to 90% of variables; backbone computation in practice via a bounded number of SAT calls.

title: Gärdenfors & Makinson, *On the Logic of Theory Change: Partial Meet Contraction and Revision Functions*, Journal of Symbolic Logic 50(2):510–530
why: The six basic revision postulates (closure, success, inclusion, vacuity, extensionality, consistency), the Levi identity, and the representation theorem that an operation satisfies the basic postulates iff it is a partial meet contraction for some selection function.

title: *Revisions of Knowledge Systems Using Epistemic Entrenchment*, TARK'88, pp. 83–95
why: Epistemic entrenchment as a stipulated ordering on sentences, and its correspondence with transitively relational partial meet contraction.

title: *On the Difference between Updating a Knowledge Base and Revising It*, KR'91, pp. 387–394
why: The separation of revision (the world is fixed, the description was wrong) from update (the world changed), and that the two satisfy different postulate sets.

title: *On the Logic of Iterated Belief Revision*, Artificial Intelligence 89:1–29
why: AGM postulates are too weak to preserve conditional beliefs across a sequence of inputs; four additional postulates C1–C4 defined over epistemic states rather than belief sets.

title: Ellie Pavlick, Burcu Karagol Ayan, Deepak Ramachandran, "Which Linguist Invented the Lightbulb? Presupposition Verification for Question-Answering", ACL 2021 (Long Papers), pp. 3932-3945
why: ~21% of unanswerable Natural Questions are explained by unverifiable presuppositions; a generate-verify-explain pipeline over a question's presuppositions is implementable, with verification the bottleneck.

title: "A Truth Maintenance System", Artificial Intelligence 12(3):231–272
why: A TMS records and maintains the reasons for a program's beliefs and traces them to find the consequences of changes in the set of assumptions; SL justifications with inlist/outlist, IN/OUT status, well-founded support, user-designated contradiction nodes, and dependency-directed backtracking with culprit selection.

title: "The Ins and Outs of Reason Maintenance", IJCAI-83, pp. 349–351
why: Doyle's own renaming of the mechanism to 'reason maintenance system' — the system maintains reasons, not truth.

title: "An Assumption-based TMS", Artificial Intelligence 28(2):127–162
why: ATMS manipulates assumption sets rather than justifications: environments, node labels (sound, complete, consistent, minimal), nogoods as minimal inconsistent environments; retraction and most backtracking avoided, context switching free.

title: "Forward reasoning and dependency-directed backtracking in a system for computer-aided circuit analysis", Artificial Intelligence 9(2):135–196
authors: Richard M. Stallman & Gerald J. Sussman
why: Origin of dependency-directed backtracking: on a conflict the search backs up far enough to remove the inconsistency, instead of discarding good choices chronologically.

title: "A Rational Reconstruction of Nonmonotonic Truth Maintenance Systems", Artificial Intelligence 43(2):219–234
why: Implementing a non-monotonic TMS is NP-complete; includes an analysis of the role of dependency-directed backtracking in dealing with contradictions.

title: *Therapist Behavior as a Determinant for Client Noncompliance: A Paradox for the Behavior Modifier*, Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 53(6)
why: Sequential dependency plus single-subject ABAB reversals: therapist 'teach' and 'confront' raise the probability of the client's next turn being non-compliant; 'facilitate' and 'support' lower it.

title: Benefield & Tonigan, *Enhancing motivation for change in problem drinking: A controlled comparison of two therapist styles*, Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 61(3), 455-461
why: 42 problem drinkers randomised to directive-confrontational vs client-centred delivery of the same feedback; the confrontational arm produced more client resistance and in-session resistance predicted drinking at one year.

title: Miller, Yahne, Palmer & Fulcher, *Client commitment language during motivational interviewing predicts drug use outcomes*, Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 71(5), 862-878
why: Strength (not frequency) of commitment language late in the session predicted proportion days abstinent; commitment strength mediated desire, ability, need and reasons.

title: *Toward a theory of motivational interviewing*, American Psychologist 64(6), 527-537
why: The relational/technical decomposition and the causal chain model linking counsellor responses, client language and post-treatment outcome — the source of the name 'technical hypothesis'.

title: *Chasing change talk: The clinician's role in evoking client language about change*, Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment 39(1), 65-70
why: ABAB analogue, 9 clinicians and 47 undergraduates: percent change talk higher in the evocation phase than the functional-analysis phase, t(46)=6.56, p<.001, d=1.19.

title: Apodaca, Borsari et al., *A meta-analysis of motivational interviewing process: Technical, relational, and conditional process models of change*, Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 86(2), 140-157
why: k=58 reports, 36 studies, 40 effect sizes, N=3,025; counsellor-behaviour to client-language paths supported, change talk non-significant as an independent predictor of outcome, sustain talk associated with worse outcome (r≈.19).

title: Rule 611(c) "Leading Questions" (Pub. L. 93-595, Jan. 2, 1975; Advisory Committee's Note, 1972; restyled 2011)
why: The rule text permitting leading questions on cross-examination and with hostile/adverse witnesses; the Advisory Committee's stated rationale that the objection rests on "the supposition that the witness is favorable to the examiner"; and that "ordinarily" exists to deny leading questions where cross-examination is "in form only and not in fact".

title: "Reconstruction of automobile destruction: An example of the interaction between language and memory", Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior 13(5):585-589
authors: Elizabeth F. Loftus & John C. Palmer
why: Substituting the verb "smashed" for "hit" in a post-event question raised speed estimates and increased false reports of broken glass that was not in the film.

title: "I don't think that's what really happened: The effect of cross-examination on the accuracy of children's reports", Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied 9(3):187-195
why: 5-6-year-olds put through cross-examination-style questioning changed previously correct answers as readily as incorrect ones, so the changes bore little relation to the truth.

title: "The effect of cross-examination on the accuracy of adult eyewitness testimony", Applied Cognitive Psychology 25(4):554-561
why: Adult witnesses cross-examined by a trainee barrister changed both initially correct and initially incorrect answers, showing negative effects of cross-examination on accuracy.

title: 399 U.S. 149, 158 (1970)
why: The Supreme Court's quotation of Wigmore's claim that cross-examination is "the greatest legal engine ever invented for the discovery of truth" — the doctrinal confidence the empirical work undercuts.

title: F. C. Pereira, W. Bialek, "The Information Bottleneck Method", Proc. 37th Annual Allerton Conference on Communication, Control and Computing, pp. 368-377 (also arXiv:physics/0004057)
why: The IB Lagrangian L = I(X̃;X) - beta I(X̃;Y), the three self-consistent equations, the claim that the KL distortion emerges from the variational principle rather than being assumed, the non-uniqueness of the converged solution, and the remark that near-lossless compression at finite beta requires the existence of sufficient statistics.

title: B. D. Tracey, S. Van Kuyk, "Caveats for Information Bottleneck in Deterministic Scenarios", ICLR 2019 (arXiv:1808.07593)
why: When Y is a deterministic function of X, the IB curve cannot be recovered by maximising the IB Lagrangian over beta and every point of the curve is attained by trivial solutions.

title: S. Sabato, N. Tishby, "Learning and generalization with the information bottleneck", Theoretical Computer Science 411(29-30):2696-2711
why: Finite-sample bounds for the plug-in empirical IB estimate, with the gap between empirical and true relevant information controlled by I(X̃;X).

title: "Agglomerative Information Bottleneck", Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 12 (NIPS 1999), pp. 617-623
why: The greedy bottom-up merge algorithm; the merger cost d(zi,zj) = (p(zi)+p(zj))·JS_Pi2[p(y|zi),p(y|zj)] equalling the exact loss of I(Z;Y) and computable in O(|Y|) per pair; AIB as the beta->infinity hard limit of the IB self-consistent equations; the output being the full hierarchy of m-partitions for m = N..1; the 20 Newsgroups result (5765 strings to 50 clusters losing ~0.1% of relevant information, to 6 clusters keeping ~90%) as a single 1999 experiment on a two-group subset; the empirically-concave information curve and the conditional 'if this is always true' stopping heuristic; the statement that the hard partition is inferior to the soft one in the information plane.

title: Subramanyam Mallela & Dharmendra S. Modha, "Information-Theoretic Co-clustering", Proc. 9th ACM SIGKDD (KDD '03), pp. 89-98
why: Co-clustering takes k and l (row/column cluster counts) as inputs; Lemma 2.1 that the loss in mutual information I(X;Y)-I(X̂;Ŷ) equals D(p(X,Y)||q(X,Y)) for a factored approximation q; Theorem 4.1 monotone decrease of the objective and Corollary 4.1 termination at a locally optimal assignment; complexity O(nz·tau·(k+l)); the quoted objection that agglomeration procedures do not scale linearly with sample size as top-down methods do; the statement that co-clustering is NP-hard and a local minimum does not guarantee a global one.

title: *Generalization as Search*, Artificial Intelligence 18(2):203–226
why: The version space is the set of hypotheses in a declared language consistent with all examples, represented by the S and G boundary sets and maintained by candidate elimination; the target is determined when S = G is a singleton; origin of the framing that an inconsistency collapses the space and that the search cannot separate an erroneous instance from a generalisation language too poor to hold the target, and of the halve-the-version-space rule for a learner-chosen instance (locator inside the paper unconfirmed; the compact wording follows the later textbook restatement, which is cited in-line and unkeyed).

title: *Quantifying Inductive Bias: AI Learning Algorithms and Valiant's Learning Framework*, Artificial Intelligence
why: Version-space boundary sets can grow exponentially in the number of instances processed, so the boundary-set representation is not a complexity guarantee.

title: Wolfman, Domingos & Weld, *Programming by Demonstration Using Version Space Algebra*, Machine Learning 53:111–156
why: Version spaces over arbitrary functions can be composed by union and join into a version space algebra, giving a compact representation of all programs consistent with a set of demonstrations (SMARTedit).

title: *Automating String Processing in Spreadsheets Using Input-Output Examples*, POPL 2011, 317–330
why: FlashFill represents the set of all consistent programs as a graph in which every path is a program, intersected against each example, so synthesis succeeds from one or two examples.

title: *Predicting a Correct Program in Programming by Example*, CAV 2015
why: Few examples leave a large set of consistent programs; selecting one requires a separately learned ranking function that the examples do not supply.

title: Conor F. Madigan, Matthew H. Moskewicz, Sharad Malik, "Efficient Conflict Driven Learning in a Boolean Satisfiability Solver", ICCAD 2001, pp. 279-285
why: antecedent clauses and the implication graph; learning schemes as bipartitions (cuts) of that graph; UIP as a vertex dominating both vertices of the conflicting variable; the asserting-clause requirement; 1UIP empirically outperforms rel_sat, GRASP, min-cut, all-UIP and decision schemes (>=2x); restarts are cheap because learned clauses persist

title: Robert C. Schrag, "Using CSP Look-Back Techniques to Solve Real-World SAT Instances", AAAI-97, pp. 203-208
why: relevance-bounded learning: bounding which learned clauses are kept is what makes look-back learning practical on large real-world instances

title: Adnan Darwiche, "On the power of clause-learning SAT solvers as resolution engines", Artificial Intelligence 175(2):512-525
why: CDCL solvers with non-deterministic branching and restarts yield proof systems that p-simulate general resolution without additional techniques

title: "The intractability of resolution", Theoretical Computer Science 39:297-308
why: the pigeonhole tautologies have no polynomial-length resolution proof, so learning cannot make every contradiction structure cheap

title: *The Sciences of the Artificial*, MIT Press (1st ed. 1969; 3rd ed. 1996, ch. 5, p. 132)
why: 'Solving a problem simply means representing it so as to make the solution transparent' - problem representation as part of problem solving (Number Scrabble / t

title: *The Pyramid Principle: Logic in Writing and Thinking*, Pitman, London, 1987 (1st ed., ISBN 9780273033455) [book]
why: MECE (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive) as the named criterion for the branches under a node, and the ch. 9 split between diagnostic frameworks (caus — verifier 2026-09-10: Correct: the 1987 Pitman edition is titled 'Logic in Writing and Thinking' (no 'Problem Solving'); ISBN 0273710516 is the 2010 3rd edition; 'Logic in Writing, T — record corrected 2026-09-10 per the verifier

title: *The McKinsey Way: Using the Techniques of the World's Top Strategic Consultants to Help You and Your Business*, McGraw-Hill [book]
why: The consulting-practice claim: MECE and the issue tree as standard McKinsey problem-solving apparatus ('a sine qua non of the problem-solving process').

title: R., Wang, P., Ma, J., Zhang, D., Sha, L., Sui, Z. — Be a Multitude to Itself: A Prompt Evolution Framework for Red Teaming (Findings of EMNLP 2024; arXiv 2502.16109)
why: RTPE (Red Teaming Prompt Evolution) evolves red-teaming prompts along two separate operators — in-breadth evolving via enhanced in-context learning, in-depth ev

title: S. C. Cheung, S. M. Yiu, 'Metamorphic Testing: A New Approach for Generating Next Test Cases', Technical Report HKUST-CS98-01, Department of Computer Science, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
why: Without a test oracle, a metamorphic relation pairs a transformation of the input with an expected consequence on the output; a violation of that relation is a

title: Gordon Fraser, Ana B. Sanchez, Antonio Ruiz-Cortes, 'A Survey on Metamorphic Testing', IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 42(9):805-824
why: Who uses metamorphic testing and where: a survey of 119 papers reporting more than twelve application areas, from web services through simulation and modelling

title: Panach & Distante, *Requirements elicitation methods based on interviews in comparison: A family of experiments*, Information and Software Technology 126:106361
why: Family of four experiments (167 subjects) in which paper prototyping elicited more requirements and higher-rated quality than unstructured interviews — the near

title: S. & Fischhoff, B. (1980). Training for calibration. Organizational Behavior and Human Performance, 26(2), 149-171.
why: 11 sessions of 200 assessments with feedback produced considerable learning, almost all of it after the first feedback; modest generalisation to some related tasks and none to two others; in Exp. 2 feedback about overconfidence lowered confidence without improving calibration or resolution (Exp. 2 detail unconfirmed against full text).

title: E. R. & Opel, R. B. (2000). Training to improve calibration and discrimination: The effects of performance and environmental feedback. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 83(2), 282-309.
why: Performance feedback reduced overconfidence; environmental feedback improved discrimination and increased overconfidence; neither improved the other component - calibration and discrimination are dissociable.

title: W., Chen, E., Mellers, B. & Tetlock, P. (2016). Developing expert political judgment: The impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments. Judgment and Decision Making, 11(5), 509-526.
why: A training module (CHAMPS KNOW: comparison classes and base rates, time series, averaging independent evidence, post-mortems, effort selection) never designed to exceed one hour improved standardised Brier scores over control in all four tournament years, by roughly 6-12%.

title: B., Ungar, L., Baron, J., Ramos, J., Gurcay, B., Fincher, K., Scott, S. E., Moore, D., Atanasov, P., Swift, S. A., Murray, T., Stone, E. & Tetlock, P. E. (2014). Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament. Psychological Science, 25(5), 1106-1115.
why: Probability training, teaming and tracking improved both calibration and resolution in a two-year geopolitical forecasting tournament; the training taught reference classes and averaging of multiple estimates.

title: C. E., Thomas, R. P., Illingworth, D. A. & Dougherty, M. R. (2025). Rethinking the role of teams and training in geopolitical forecasting: The effect of uncontrolled method variance on statistical conclusions. Psychological Science, 36(1), 3-18.
why: Re-analysis of the same tournament under an item-response model of latent forecasting ability: once extraneous method variance is controlled, the best-fitting models across the first two years substantially reduce, eliminate, or in places reverse the teaming and training effects.

title: A. H. & Winkler, R. L. (1977). Reliability of subjective probability forecasts of precipitation and temperature. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C (Applied Statistics), 26(1), 41-47.
why: Operational weather forecasters do produce reliable (calibrated) subjective probability forecasts of precipitation occurrence and temperature - calibration arising from a repeated question with prompt scored outcomes rather than from training.

title: *The Scientific Image*, Oxford: Clarendon Press, ch. 5 "The Pragmatics of Explanation"
why: An explanation is an answer to a why-question; a why-question is the triple <topic Pk, contrast class X, relevance relation R>, presupposing that Pk is true, that only Pk in X is true, and that some proposition bears R to <Pk,X>; R varies with the kind of reason requested and is not otherwise constrained.

title: "Contrastive Explanation", Royal Institute of Philosophy Supplements 27 (Explanation and its Limits), 247-266, Cambridge University Press
why: The Difference Condition: to explain why P rather than Q, cite a causal difference between P and not-Q - a cause of P and the absence of a corresponding event in the history of not-Q; and the argument that finding the difference is a cognitively simpler problem than producing a complete cause.

title: "Explanation in artificial intelligence: Insights from the social sciences", Artificial Intelligence 267:1-38 (arXiv:1706.07269)
why: The four findings of the review: explanations are contrastive (sought against counterfactual foils); selected in a biased manner, people rarely expect an actual and complete cause; probabilities probably don't matter - referring to probabilities or statistical relationships is not as effective as referring to causes; explanations are social. Plus the motivating claim that most XAI work uses only the researchers' intuition of what a good explanation is.

title: "Information Structure in Discourse: Towards an Integrated Formal Theory of Pragmatics", OSU Working Papers in Linguistics 49 (1996; rev. 1998); reprinted as "Information structure: Towards an integrated formal theory of pragmatics", Semantics and Pragmatics 5(6), 2012
why: The InfoStr tuple <M,Q,A,<,Acc,CG,QUD>; QUD as a push-down stack of accepted, as-yet-unanswered, answerable questions with the entailment clause (c); the immediate QUD as last(QUD(m)); the definition of Relevance (a move is Relevant to the QUD iff it introduces a partial answer or is part of a strategy to answer it); partial vs complete answer over the Q-alternative set; the strategy of inquiry Strat(q); the Big Question; popping a question when answered or determined practically unanswerable; implicit QUDs retrieved by accommodation and presupposed by prosodic focus.

title: "Discourse integration guided by the 'Question under Discussion'", Cognitive Psychology 65(2):352-379
why: Three eye-movement experiments: reading of a following verb phrase was disrupted when it failed to resolve an implicit QUD relative to the same material with no clear QUD — evidence for online use of the QUD in comprehension.

title: Ritika Mangla, Greg Durrett & Junyi Jessy Li, "QUDeval: The Evaluation of Questions Under Discussion Discourse Parsing", EMNLP 2023 (arXiv:2310.14520)
why: First evaluation framework for automatic QUD parsing: 2,190 QUD questions from fine-tuned systems and LLMs judged on answer compatibility, givenness and anchor relevance; satisfying all QUD constraints remained challenging for the models tested while human-authored QUDs scored highly.

title: "On optimum recognition error and reject tradeoff", IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 16(1):41–46
why: The optimal reject rule for a known posterior is a single threshold on the maximum posterior set by an explicitly named cost of rejection; the error rate is recoverable from the reject function.

title: "Classification with reject option", Canadian Journal of Statistics 34(4):709–721
authors: R. Herbei and M. H. Wegkamp
why: Binary classification with a reject option: the classifier reports 'I don't know' when the conditional class probabilities are too close to separate.

title: "On the Foundations of Noise-free Selective Classification", JMLR 11:1605–1641
why: Definition of a selective model as a pair (f,g), of coverage φ(g)=E[g(x)] and selective risk R(f,g)=E[ℓ(f(x),y)g(x)]/φ(g), and of the risk–coverage trade-off curve.

title: "Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks", NeurIPS 30
why: The SGR algorithm searches a confidence threshold on held-out data and returns a selective classifier with a risk bound; abstract reports 2% top-5 ImageNet error guaranteed with probability 99.9% at almost 60% coverage.

title: D. Průša and V. Voráček, "Optimal Strategies for Reject Option Classifiers", JMLR 24(11)
why: The cost-based, bounded-improvement and bounded-coverage rejection models lead to the same prediction strategy (a Bayes classifier with a randomised Bayes selection function); the 'proper uncertainty score' is defined as the scalar summary sufficient to build that selection function and is learned separately for a black-box classifier.

title: "Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know", arXiv:2207.05221
why: Models can be trained to predict P(IK) and partially generalise across tasks, but calibrate poorly on new tasks.

title: P., Murakhovs'ka, L., Xiong, C., Wu, C.-S. — Are You Sure? Challenging LLMs Leads to Performance Drops in The FlipFlop Experiment (arXiv 2311.08596)
why: Across ten LLMs and seven classification tasks, models flip their answers 46% of the time on average when challenged with 'are you sure?', with an average 17% accuracy drop between first and final prediction; finetuning on synthetic data reduces the deterioration by 60% without removing it.

title: A., Goldberg, J., Agarwal, A. A., Lin, J., Zhou, A., Daneshjou, R., Koyejo, S. — SycEval: Evaluating LLM Sycophancy (arXiv 2502.08177; AAAI/ACM AIES 2025)
why: Capitulation under rebuttal in 58.19% of cases across ChatGPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet and Gemini-1.5-Pro on AMPS and MedQuAD; 43.52% progressive (wrong→right) and 14.66% regressive (right→wrong); preemptive rebuttals capitulate more than in-context (61.75% vs 56.52%) and citation-based rebuttals give the highest regressive rate.

title: J., Huang, D., Lu, Y., Zhou, D., Le, Q. V. — Simple synthetic data reduces sycophancy in large language models (arXiv 2308.03958)
why: Models agree with a user's stated view on statements that are objectively incorrect (simple addition); both model scaling (PaLM to 540B) and instruction tuning increase sycophancy; a lightweight synthetic-data finetune reduces it on held-out prompts.

title: M., Yu, S., Lee, C., Khadpe, P., Ibrahim, L., Jurafsky, D. — ELEPHANT: Measuring and understanding social sycophancy in LLMs (arXiv 2505.13995)
why: Social sycophancy — excessive preservation of the user's face on items with no ground truth — is a distinct measured object: on perspective-flipped moral conflicts models affirm both sides in 48% of cases, and preserve face ~45 points more than humans.

title: Karl G. D. Bailey, Fernanda Ferreira, "Do speakers and listeners observe the Gricean Maxim of Quantity?", Journal of Memory and Language 54(4):554-573
why: Three experiments: speakers over-describe almost one-third of the time; listeners do not judge over-descriptions worse than concise expressions; Visual World Paradigm shows over-descriptions trigger eye movements interpretable as confusion; 'people are only moderately Gricean'.

title: "Predicting pragmatic reasoning in language games", Science 336:998
authors: Michael C. Frank & Noah D. Goodman
why: Referential communication games modelled by assuming speakers attempt to be informative and listeners recover intended referents by Bayesian inference; close, parameter-free fit to human judgements.

title: "Precis of Relevance: Communication and Cognition", Behavioral and Brain Sciences 10(4):697-754
why: The single principle of relevance is 'enough on its own' to account for disambiguation, reference assignment, recovery of implicatures and other underdetermined aspects of interpretation — a rival to the four-maxim structure.

title: DoD News Briefing, 12 February 2002 (transcript)
why: The known knowns / known unknowns / unknown unknowns trichotomy as stated in public discourse; Rumsfeld names three states, not four.

title: *The Johari Window: a Graphic Model of Interpersonal Awareness*, Proceedings of the Western Training Laboratory in Group Development, UCLA Extension Office
why: The 2x2 grid of known/not-known crossed over self and others — the earlier form of the knowledge matrix; cited from secondary literature, marked [?] in ## Limits. — verifier 2026-09-10: No official primary listing (no DOI, publisher page or digitised proceedings); only consistent secondary citations. Existence plausible, not confirmed.

title: *What Rumsfeld Doesn't Know That He Knows About Abu Ghraib*, In These Times
why: The fourth cell, the 'unknown known', is Žižek's addition to Rumsfeld's three states, read as disavowed knowledge.

title: Krause & Ray, *Near-Optimal Bayesian Active Learning with Noisy Observations*, NIPS 23
why: Generalized binary search, near-optimal in the noise-free case, can perform very poorly when observations are noisy; a different objective (EC2) is needed to recover a competitiveness guarantee.

title: *Bayesian Experimental Design: A Review*, Statistical Science 10(3), 273-304
why: BED criteria are special cases of one decision-theoretic utility framework; attribution for the decision-theoretic criterion family

title: *Optimum Experimental Designs*, JRSS Series B 21(2), 272-304
why: classical (non-Bayesian) optimal design theory and the D-/A-optimality criteria defined on the information matrix

title: *Comparison of Experiments*, Proceedings of the Second Berkeley Symposium on Mathematical Statistics and Probability, 93-102
why: Introduces the comparison of experiments and the sufficiency criterion: if one experiment is sufficient for another, it is more informative. Cited in the body; not yet in the note's frontmatter because the key is not in sources.json.

title: "Causes and Strategies for Requesting Clarification in Dialogue", Proceedings of the 5th SIGdial Workshop on Discourse and Dialogue, HLT-NAACL 2004, pp. 136-143 (ACL Anthology W04-2325)
why: A CR is about a previous utterance rather than the world; the three classification dimensions level / severity / extent; the four Clark-Allwood levels and their fine-grained refinement; extending confidence scores to every processing stage; the reject / confirm (explicit or implicit) / accept strategy; the proof-of-concept status of the implementation and the undetermined combination rule.

title: "Clarification, Ellipsis, and the Nature of Contextual Updates in Dialogue", Linguistics and Philosophy 27(3):297-365
why: The clausal and constituent readings of a clarification request, and the result that contextual updates from an utterance cannot be defined in purely semantic terms because resolving clarification ellipsis requires operations on the antecedent utterance's form.

title: Karl Mulligan, Todd Snider, Robert D. Hawkins & Michael Franke, "Act or Clarify? Modeling Sensitivity to Uncertainty and Cost in Communication", CogSci 2026 (arXiv:2602.02843)
why: Expected-regret model of the decision to ask a clarification question; two experiments in which uncertainty and action cost interact in driving clarification-seeking.

title: Sean G. Roberts, Julija Baranova, Joe Blythe, Paul Drew, Simeon Floyd et al., "Universal Principles in the Repair of Communication Problems", PLoS ONE 10(9): e0136100
why: Other-initiated repair is used on average about once per 1.4 minutes, in a sample of 12 languages from 8 language families — cited to distinguish it as a separately measured object from the dialogue-systems clarification request.

title: S. & Mandel, D. R. (2025). Calibration feedback with the Practical scoring rule does not improve calibration of confidence. Futures & Foresight Science, 7(1), e199. doi:10.1002/ffo2.199
why: Two experiments (N1=610, N2=871) comparing control, outcome feedback and performance feedback scored by the Practical scoring rule found no improvement in calibration from either training regime; calibration overall was predicted by Actively Open-Minded Thinking but its change across blocks was not.

title: W. K., Doherty, M. E. & O'Connor, R., Jr. (1989). Effects of cognitive feedback on performance. Psychological Bulletin, 106, 410-433.
why: Cognitive feedback decomposes into task information, cognitive information and functional validity information; the task-information component appeared responsible for performance improvements in multiple-cue probability learning, in contrast to outcome feedback.

title: S. (2018). Calibration Scoring Rules for Practical Prediction Training. arXiv:1808.07501
why: The 'Practical' scoring rules are designed for calibration training - intuitive in a right/wrong prediction context, with desiderata beyond properness aimed at usability and learning efficiency.

title: S. & Fischhoff, B. (1981). The Effects of Gender and Instructions on Calibration. Decision Research Technical Report PTR-1092-81-7 (DTIC AD-A102255).
why: Two groups assessed confidence on 200 general-knowledge questions; one got brief instructions, one got three single-spaced pages explaining calibration explicitly ('we want you to be well calibrated in the same sense that a thermometer is well calibrated'). 'The instructions had no statistically significant effect on any measure'; most subjects were overconfident either way. Full text read via the Internet Archive mirror of the DTIC report.

title: S., Fischhoff, B. & Phillips, L. D. (1982). Calibration of probabilities: The state of the art to 1980. Technical report, DTIC AD-A101986; also in Kahneman, Slovic & Tversky (eds), Judgment under Uncertainty, CUP, 306-334.
why: The authors' own review of Lichtenstein & Fischhoff (1980): 'appreciable improvement in calibration, all of which occurred between the first and the second session'; modest generalisation across difficulty, content and response mode, 'but no improvement was found with a fractile assessment task ... or on the discrimination of European from American handwriting samples'. Also reports Fischhoff & Slovic (1980): discouraging instructions on an Asian-vs-European children's drawings task 'lowered the mean response by about .05' yet 'substantial overconfidence was still found'. Full text read.

title: Emanuel A. Schegloff & Gail Jefferson, "A Simplest Systematics for the Organization of Turn-Taking for Conversation", Language 50(4): 696-735
why: The turn-taking system has as a by-product a proof procedure: a next turn is built on what its speaker took the prior turn to be doing, and so publicly displays that understanding.

title: Gail Jefferson & Harvey Sacks, "The Preference for Self-Correction in the Organization of Repair in Conversation", Language 53(2): 361-382
why: Repair is an organization over trouble in speaking, hearing and understanding, structured by who initiates and in which position; opportunities for self-initiation precede those for other-initiation, and there is a strong empirical skew toward self-repair.

title: "Repair After Next Turn: The Last Structurally Provided Defense of Intersubjectivity in Conversation", American Journal of Sociology 97(5): 1295-1345
why: Third position — the turn after the recipient's response — is where the trouble-source speaker repairs its own prior turn on evidence of misunderstanding displayed by that response, and is the last structurally provided defense of intersubjectivity; the paper also names a rarer fourth position, and describes the third-position turn's components (initiator, acceptance, rejection of the displayed understanding, repair proper).

title: B. & Slovic, P. (1980). A little learning...: Confidence in multicue judgment tasks. In R. Nickerson (ed.), Attention and Performance VIII, 779-800. Erlbaum. Read as Decision Research technical report PTR-1060-78-6 (DTIC AD-A059147), June 1978, via the Internet Archive mirror.
why: Experiment 5: 92 subjects, European-vs-Asian children's drawings, accuracy 54.1%/52.3% against mean confidence .667/.677. Experiment 6: 76 subjects, same task with a changed cover story ('many people have claimed that the art of small children is the same in all cultural settings; others disagree') plus discouraging response instructions ('it may well be impossible to make this sort of discrimination ... do not hesitate to respond with .5 for every one of them'); 'the change in instructions had some effect in the appropriate direction, reducing the mean confidence of both groups by approximately .05' to .631/.627, accuracy 57.7%/45.6%, both groups still overconfident; 'Only 6 of 76 subjects (4 in the labels group, 2 in the no-labels group) accepted the option of responding with .5 to all items.' Figures quoted from the DTIC report and not independently confirmed against the published chapter [?].

title: B. (1982). Debiasing. In D. Kahneman, P. Slovic & A. Tversky (eds), Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases, 422-444. Cambridge University Press.
why: The classification of debiasing strategies by source of bias, and the escalating four-step sequence for 'faulty judges': warn about the possibility of bias, describe the bias, provide personalised feedback, train extensively.

title: D., Doll, D. & Mohnen, A. (2017). Caution! Warnings as a useless countermeasure to reduce overconfidence? An experimental evaluation in light of enhanced and dynamic warning designs. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making 30(2), 347-358. doi:10.1002/bdm.1946
why: Two experiments on overconfidence in interval estimates arguing the warning null must be re-read in light of warning design; repeated (dynamic) warnings, as against a single static one, have the potential to reduce overestimation. Read from abstract and secondary description only; full text paywalled [?].

title: Bodík & Larus, *Mining Specifications*, POPL '02, pp. 4–16
why: The term and the pipeline (tracer, flow-dependence annotator, scenario extractor, PFSA learner + corer); the assumption, stated in the abstract and introduction, that an executing program generally uses an API or ADT correctly even when it contains errors, so common behaviour reveals the protocol; the expert-supplied definer/user table, scenario seeds, object bound and corer cutoff; heat as traversal likelihood computed as a Markov-chain problem rather than raw edge weight; the three problem statements (exact miner unsolvable, identification in the limit undecidable, PFSA approximation not efficiently learnable, efficient only for acyclic deterministic targets) and the use of a greedy learner with no approximation guarantee; the X11 experiment on 16 client programs, 4 programs not inspected by the expert, corer/expert disagreement on 5 of 27 states.

title: Mandelin, Bodík & Larus, *Debugging Temporal Specifications with Concept Analysis*, PLDI '03, p. 182ff
why: Specification miners produce buggy specifications, so a mined specification must itself be debugged; the Cable tool cut one debugging case from 224 human decisions to 28, on average under one third as many decisions as inspecting all traces.

title: *Language Identification in the Limit*, Information and Control 10, pp. 447–474
why: Identification of regular languages in the limit is not possible in the setting Ammons et al. reduce their Problem 2.3 to; cited here as the ground of that undecidability claim.

title: R. S. — Question-Negotiation and Information Seeking in Libraries. College & Research Libraries 29(3):178–194 (1968); read in the 75th-anniversary reprint, C&RL 76(3):251–267, doi:10.5860/crl.76.3.251
why: The four levels Q1 visceral / Q2 conscious / Q3 formalized / Q4 compromised as points on a 'question spectrum'; Q4 as the question 'recast in anticipation of what the files can deliver'; that an inquirer who does not know the specialist poses Q4 while one who accepts him as a colleague lets negotiation start earlier; the answerer's job of working back to Q3 and possibly Q2; the command/question distinction and the claim that the second assumption (the asker knows the system's functional organisation) is not valid; the five filters; the interview basis and the statement that quantitative data on the process is non-existent.

title: R. S. — The process of asking questions. American Documentation 13(4):391–396, doi:10.1002/asi.5090130405
why: Origin of the four levels of question formation; cited on the strength of Taylor's own 1968 restatement and the journal abstract — the 1962 text was not read this pass, and the note says so in ## Limits.

title: Guyatt G, Oxman AD, Alderson P, Dahm P, Falck-Ytter Y, et al. GRADE guidelines: 14. Going from evidence to recommendations: the significance and presentation of recommendations. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 66(7):719-725. doi:10.1016/j.jclinepi.2012.03.013
why: Strength of a recommendation is the extent to which one can be confident that the desirable consequences of an intervention outweigh its undesirable consequences; it is a binary strong/weak (conditional, discretionary, qualified) cut of an underlying continuum, graded separately from confidence in effect estimates, and carries a published implication table for patients, clinicians and policy makers.

title: Schunemann HJ, Oxman AD, Pottie K, Meerpohl JJ, Alonso Coello P, et al. GRADE guidelines: 15. Going from evidence to recommendation - determinants of a recommendation's direction and strength. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 66(7):726-735. doi:10.1016/j.jclinepi.2013.02.003

Both PhilPapers/PhilArchive mirrors (philpapers.org/archive/WHIIAA-6.pdf and the WHIIAA-7.pdf that Unpaywall itself lists as the paper's open-access location) return a Cloudflare "Just a moment..." bot-wall to every fetch method tried, including a public reader-proxy (r.jina.ai). The abstract (verified identically via four independent extractions: direct fetch, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex) states only that the paper builds a framework on inferential erotetic logic and "explores several norms... some sympathetically, others unsympathetically" — it names no specific norm, theorem, or example, so nothing in it passes "what is the actual claim, under what conditions, who established it." Search-engine synthesis repeatedly attached an "Evoked Question Norm" to this 2023 paper, but tracing it shows that norm is the contribution of a different, later paper (Willard-Kyle, Millson & Whitcomb, "Evoked Questions and Inquiring Attitudes", Philosophical Quarterly 2026) that only cites this one's erotetic-logic background as prior art — writing a note under the whitcomb-2023 key using that content would misattribute a claim never verified as this paper's own. title: Aaditya Ramdas, Alessandro Rinaldo, "E-detectors: A Nonparametric Framework for Sequential Change Detection", The New England Journal of Statistics in Data Science 2(2):229–260 (DOI 10.51387/23-NEJSDS51; arXiv:2203.03532)
why: An e-detector is a sum of e-processes (a generalization of nonnegative supermartingales) started at consecutive times; it gives nonasymptotic average-run-length bounds when the pre- and post-change distributions are nonparametrically specified and composite, near-optimal detection-delay bounds only in cases such as sub-Gaussian or sub-exponential, and recovers the classical likelihood-based procedures (CUSUM, Shiryaev–Roberts) in parametric problems.

title: Ivan Petej, Ilia Nouretdinov, Ernst Ahlberg, Lars Carlsson, Alex Gammerman, "Retrain or not retrain: conformal test martingales for change-point detection" (COPA 2021, PMLR 152; arXiv:2102.10439)
why: Conformal test martingales are processes that are martingales under any exchangeable distribution for the data; they can be applied on top of any prediction algorithm to detect when the data distribution has changed (when to retrain), with validity guaranteed and efficiency described by the authors as a first exploration.

title: "Testing Randomness Online", Statistical Science 36(4) (DOI 10.1214/20-STS817)

title: Yao Xie, Hanjun Dai, Le Song, "Scan B-statistic for kernel change-point detection", Sequential Analysis 38(4):503–544
why: A computationally efficient kernel change-point detection statistic: the unbiased MMD between the most recent block of B observations and N pre-change reference blocks, averaged and variance-normalised, at O(NB²) per sample, with the tail probability characterised by a change-of-measure argument so the average run length can be targeted analytically. (Read this pass through Wei & Xie's restatement, not in full.)

title: Yao Xie, "Online Kernel CUSUM for Change-Point Detection" (arXiv:2211.15070)

title: J. V. & Petrusic, W. M. (1994). The calibration and resolution of confidence in perceptual judgments. Perception & Psychophysics, 55(4), 412–428. DOI 10.3758/BF03205299

Read from the published abstract via Europe PMC (PMID 8036121); full text not obtained.

Read from the Europe PMC abstract record; full text not obtained.

title: H. & Winman, A. (1996). Underconfidence in sensory discrimination: The interaction between experimental setting and response strategies. Perception & Psychophysics, 58(3), 374–382. DOI 10.3758/BF03206813

title: J. V. & Petrusic, W. M. (1999). Realism of confidence in sensory discrimination. Perception & Psychophysics, 61(7), 1369–1383. DOI 10.3758/BF03206187

title: P. & Olsson, H. (1997). Thurstonian and Brunswikian origins of uncertainty in judgment: A sampling model of confidence in sensory discrimination. Psychological Review, 104(2), 344–366. DOI 10.1037/0033-295X.104.2.344

Table 1(b): K=5, one-sided α=0.05 boundaries — O'Brien–Fleming 3.92…1.75, Pocock constant 2.12. The law-of-the-iterated-logarithm statement pr{B(t) ≥ c√t for some t ∈ (0,1]} = 1 for any c (§3). The remark that α*_1 is very conservative early for large K and the 3.5 cap. The Discussion's statement that optimality of α* was not defined or considered. §1's attributions to Armitage et al. 1969, Pocock 1977, O'Brien & Fleming 1979, and Slud & Wei 1982's dependent increments. §4's recommendation of the Lan–Simon–Halperin conditional-power lower boundary.

title: Megan C. Grieco, Kevin Rubenstein, Jing Wang, Michael A. Proschan, *Futility Monitoring in Clinical Trials*, Statistics in Medicine 44(13–14): e70157 (PMCID PMC12153251)
why: The precise statement of the Lan–Simon–Halperin bound: under continuous monitoring with CP computed under the originally hypothesised treatment effect and stopping when CP ≤ Γ, the type II error rate is β/(1−Γ); worked case β=0.1, Γ=0.2 → 0.125. Also: Γ ≤ 0.2 as the usual choice; that re-claiming unspent α from a non-binding futility boundary inflates type I error; and the enumeration of futility-rule variants (conditional power under the design alternative vs under the observed trend, predictive power, beta spending) used in the Known as rows. This paper does not cite Chang & Chuang-Stein (2004); that claim is carried by its own key, chang-2004. — verifier 2026-09-14: does NOT support the cited claim

title: Christy Chuang-Stein, *Type I error and power in trials with one interim futility analysis*, Pharmaceutical Statistics 3(1): 51–59
why: Cited in stochastic-curtailment's Limits for exactly this: a binding interim futility analysis in a superiority trial reduces the overall type I error below the nominal level, and the authors propose setting the final analysis's significance level higher than the allowable type I error rate to recover it (for both one-sided and two-sided testing). Only metadata and the abstract-level finding were checked — author names, journal, volume 3, issue 1, pages 51–59, year 2004 and DOI 10.1002/pst.93 confirmed via Crossref; the full text is paywalled and was not read, and no other source in the note cites it. Running the four-question test: the claim (bidirectional QA-MQG alignment + contrastive learning improves automatic/human-judged question quality) holds only under supervised training on a dataset where the target answer and supporting documents are already fixed — there is no uncertainty over |W| in this setting at all, since the answer the question must yield is given as training input, not discovered. It therefore does not change how an asker selects, formulates, or evaluates a question under uncertainty (stall 2 or any other stall): it is a dataset-synthesis / reading-comprehension pretext technique, the field's own agenda. No criterion separable from the training method (e.g., round-trip QA-consistency as a proxy for question quality) is novel here — it is a known idea in QG literature applied as a training loss rather than a post-hoc filter, and the paper does not state it as a general, architecture-independent scoring rule usable outside training. title: KRAL: Knowledge and Reasoning Augmented Learning for LLM-assisted Clinical Antimicrobial Therapy
abstract: Clinical antimicrobial therapy requires the dynamic integration of pathogen profiles,host factors, pharmacological properties of antimicrobials,and the severity of infection. This complexity imposes fundamental limitations on the applicability of Large Language Models (LLMs) in high-stakes clinical decision-making including knowledge gaps, data privacy concerns, high deployment costs, and limited reasoning capabilities. To address these challenges, we propose KRAL (Knowledge and Reasoning Augmented Learning), a low-cost, scalable, privacy-preserving paradigm that leverages teacher-model reasoning to automatically distill knowledge and reasoning trajectories via answer-to-question reverse generation, employs heuristic learning for semi-supervised data augmentation (reducing manual annotation requirements by approximately 80%), and utilizes agentic reinforcement learning to jointly enhance medical knowledge and reasoning while optimizing computational and memory efficiency. A hierarchical evaluation employing diverse teacher-model proxies reduces assessment costs, while modular interface design facilitates seamless system updates. Experimental results demonstrate that KRAL significantly outperforms traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) methods. title: JudgeBoard: Benchmarking and Enhancing Small Language Models for Reasoning Evaluation
abstract: While small language models (SLMs) have shown promise on various reasoning tasks, their ability to judge the correctness of answers remains unclear compared to large language models (LLMs). Prior work on LLM-as-a-judge frameworks typically relies on comparing candidate answers against ground-truth labels or other candidate answers using predefined metrics like entailment. However, this approach is inherently indirect and difficult to fully automate, offering limited support for fine-grained and scalable evaluation of reasoning outputs. In this work, we propose JudgeBoard, a novel evaluation pipeline that directly queries models to assess the correctness of candidate answers without requiring extra answer comparisons. We focus on two core reasoning domains: mathematical reasoning and science/commonsense reasoning, and construct task-specific evaluation leaderboards using both accuracy-based ranking and an Elo-based rating system across five benchmark datasets, enabling consistent model comparison as judges rather than comparators. To improve judgment performance in lightweight models, we propose MAJ (Multi-Agent Judging), a novel multi-agent evaluation framework that leverages multiple interacting SLMs with distinct reasoning profiles to approximate LLM-level judgment accuracy through collaborative deliberation. title: Click2Graph: Interactive Panoptic Video Scene Graphs from a Single Click
abstract: State-of-the-art Video Scene Graph Generation (VSGG) systems provide structured visual understanding but operate as closed, feed-forward pipelines with no ability to incorporate human guidance. In contrast, promptable segmentation models such as SAM2 enable precise user interaction but lack semantic or relational reasoning. We introduce Click2Graph, the first interactive framework for Panoptic Video Scene Graph Generation (PVSG) that unifies visual prompting with spatial, temporal, and semantic understanding. From a single user cue, such as a click or bounding box, Click2Graph segments and tracks the subject across time, autonomously discovers interacting objects, and predicts <subject, object, predicate> triplets to form a temporally consistent scene graph. Our framework introduces two key components: a Dynamic Interaction Discovery Module that generates subject-conditioned object prompts, and a Semantic Classification Head that performs joint entity and predicate reasoning. Experiments on the OpenPVSG benchmark demonstrate that Click2Graph establishes a strong foundation for user-guided PVSG, showing how human prompting can be combined with panoptic grounding and relational inference to enable controllable and interpretable video scene understanding.

title: Adaptive multi-view feature selection for human motion retrieval
abstract: Human motion retrieval plays an important role in many motion data based applications. In the past, many researchers tended to use a single type of visual feature as data representation. Because different visual feature describes different aspects about motion data, and they have dissimilar discriminative power with respect to one particular class of human motion, it led to poor retrieval performance. Thus, it would be beneficial to combine multiple visual features together for motion data representation. In this article, we present an Adaptive Multi-view Feature Selection (AMFS) method for human motion retrieval. Specifically, we first use a local linear regression model to automatically learn multiple view-based Laplacian graphs for preserving the local geometric structure of motion data. Then, these graphs are combined together with a non-negative view-weight vector to exploit the complementary information between different features. Finally, in order to discard the redundant and irrelevant feature components from the original high-dimensional feature representation, we formulate the objective function of AMFS as a general trace ratio optimization problem, and design an effective algorithm to solve the corresponding optimization problem. Extensive experiments on two public human motion database, i.e., HDM05 and MSR Action3D, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed AMFS over the state-of-art methods for motion data retrieval. title: Joint Optimization Framework Combining Sparse Representation and Dense Retrieval in PubMed Retrieval
abstract: The exponential growth of biomedical literature indexed in PubMed has necessitated thedevelopment of advanced information retrieval systems capable of navigating complexterminologies and user intents. Traditional sparse retrieval models, such as BM25, excel atexact lexical matching but fail to capture semantic nuances, whereas emerging denseretrieval techniques utilizing transformer-based encoders offer semantic understanding butoften struggle with precise entity matching and out-of-vocabulary domain-specific terms.This paper proposes a novel framework that jointly optimizes sparse representations anddense retrieval vectors within a unified learning objective. By integrating a sparsityinducing regularization term into the dense encoder training phase, our model learns toretain critical lexical features while simultaneously projecting documents into a semanticvector space. We demonstrate that this hybrid approach mitigates the vocabulary mismatchproblem inherent in biomedical queries without requiring heavy post-hoc reranking stages.Extensive experiments conducted on standard biomedical information retrieval benchmarksreveal that the proposed framework significantly outperforms strong baselines, offering arobust solution for precision-critical medical search tasks. The results suggest that thesynergistic combination of lexical exactness and semantic flexibility is essential for the nextgeneration of biomedical search engines.

title: Uni-Retrieval: A Multi-Style Retrieval Framework for STEM's Education
abstract: In AI-facilitated teaching, leveraging various query styles to interpret abstract text descriptions is crucial for ensuring high-quality teaching. However, current retrieval models primarily focus on natural text-image retrieval, making them insufficiently tailored to educational scenarios due to the ambiguities in the retrieval process. In this paper, we propose a diverse expression retrieval task tailored to educational scenarios, supporting retrieval based on multiple query styles and expressions. We introduce the STEM Education Retrieval Dataset (SER), which contains over 24,000 query pairs of different styles, and the Uni-Retrieval, an efficient and style-diversified retrieval vision-language model based on prompt tuning. Uni-Retrieval extracts query style features as prototypes and builds a continuously updated Prompt Bank containing prompt tokens for diverse queries. This bank can updated during test time to represent domain-specific knowledge for different subject retrieval scenarios. Our framework demonstrates scalability and robustness by dynamically retrieving prompt tokens based on prototype similarity, effectively facilitating learning for unknown queries. Experimental results indicate that Uni-Retrieval outperforms existing retrieval models in most retrieval tasks. This advancement provides a scalable and precise solution for diverse educational needs.

title: Retrieval-Enhanced Machine Learning: Synthesis and Opportunities
abstract: In the field of language modeling, models augmented with retrieval components have emerged as a promising solution to address several challenges faced in the natural language processing (NLP) field, including knowledge grounding, interpretability, and scalability. Despite the primary focus on NLP, we posit that the paradigm of retrieval-enhancement can be extended to a broader spectrum of machine learning (ML) such as computer vision, time series prediction, and computational biology. Therefore, this work introduces a formal framework of this paradigm, Retrieval-Enhanced Machine Learning (REML), by synthesizing the literature in various domains in ML with consistent notations which is missing from the current literature. Also, we found that while a number of studies employ retrieval components to augment their models, there is a lack of integration with foundational Information Retrieval (IR) research. We bridge this gap between the seminal IR research and contemporary REML studies by investigating each component that comprises the REML framework. Ultimately, the goal of this work is to equip researchers across various disciplines with a comprehensive, formally structured framework of retrieval-enhanced models, thereby fostering interdisciplinary future research.

title: MegaPairs: Massive Data Synthesis For Universal Multimodal Retrieval
abstract: Despite the rapidly growing demand for multimodal retrieval, progress in this field remains severely constrained by a lack of training data. In this paper, we introduce MegaPairs, a novel data synthesis method that leverages vision language models (VLMs) and open-domain images, together with a massive synthetic dataset generated from this method. Our empirical analysis shows that MegaPairs generates high-quality data, enabling the multimodal retriever to significantly outperform the baseline model trained on 70$\times$ more data from existing datasets. Moreover, since MegaPairs solely relies on general image corpora and open-source VLMs, it can be easily scaled up, enabling continuous improvements in retrieval performance. In this stage, we produced more than 26 million training instances and trained several models of varying sizes using this data. These new models achieve state-of-the-art zero-shot performance across 4 popular composed image retrieval (CIR) benchmarks and the highest overall performance on the 36 datasets provided by MMEB. They also demonstrate notable performance improvements with additional downstream fine-tuning. Our produced dataset, well-trained models, and data synthesis pipeline will be made publicly available to facilitate the future development of this field.

title: Pre-retrieval Query Clustering for Adaptive Top-k Document Retrieval in RAG Systems
abstract: RAG systems commonly retrieve a fixed number of documents (top-k) to ground generation, but this static approach is brittle: simple queries suffer over-retrieval (adding noise and cost) while complex queries are under-retrieved, causing recall failures that cascade into incorrect answers. Motivated by the question of how many documents must be retrieved to answer an arbitrary query reliably, we propose a practical, general framework for query-adaptive retrieval depth. Offline, we estimate per-query retrieval difficulty by measuring NDCG under the default retriever and deriving a query-specific saturation point k* from the NDCG-k curve. Because computing these signals online is expensive, we cluster a large set of queries in embedding space and summarize each cluster with a recommended retrieval depth that targets high coverage (e.g., ~95%) using a mean-plus-variance rule. At runtime, the system assigns an incoming query to a cluster and selects the corresponding top-k in constant time. Compared with post-retrieval confidence methods that rely on clustering retrieved documents, our approach is pre-retrieval and query-centric, making it robust in heterogeneous, case-like corpora and applicable across domains such as legal, healthcare, finance, and enterprise search. Finally, this framework has been tested in full-traffic queries that improved $F_1$ by over 36% while reducing token usage by 14% on low-complexity clusters without accuracy loss.

title: Guaranteeing Knowledge Integration with Joint Decoding for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) significantly enhances Large Language Models (LLMs) by providing access to external knowledge. However, current research primarily focuses on retrieval quality, often overlooking the critical ''integration bottleneck'': even when relevant documents are retrieved, LLMs frequently fail to utilize them effectively due to conflicts with their internal parametric knowledge. In this paper, we argue that implicitly resolving this conflict in a single generation pass is suboptimal. We introduce GuarantRAG, a framework that explicitly decouples reasoning from evidence integration. First, we generate an ''Inner-Answer'' based solely on parametric knowledge to capture the model's reasoning flow. Second, to guarantee faithful evidence extraction, we generate a ''Refer-Answer'' using a novel Contrastive DPO objective. This objective treats the parametric Inner-Answer as a negative constraint and the retrieved documents as positive ground truth, forcing the model to suppress internal hallucinations in favor of external evidence during this phase. Finally, rather than naive concatenation or using the DPO trained model directly, we propose a joint decoding mechanism that dynamically fuses the logical coherence of the Inner-Answer with the factual precision of the Refer-Answer at the token level. title: The role of document structure and citation analysis in literature information retrieval
abstract: Literature Information Retrieval (IR) is the task of searching relevant publications given a particular information need expressed as a set of queries. With the staggering growth of scientific literature, it is critical to design effective retrieval solutions to facilitate efficient access to them. We hypothesize that particular genre specific characteristics of scientific literature such as metadata and citations are potentially helpful for enhancing scientific literature search. We conducted systematic and extensive IR experiments on open information retrieval test collections to investigate their roles in enhancing literature information retrieval effectiveness. This thesis consists of three major parts of studies. First, we examined the role of document structure in literature search through comprehensive studies on the retrieval effectiveness of a set of structure-aware retrieval models on ad hoc scientific literature search tasks. Second, under the language modeling retrieval framework, we studied exploiting citation and co-citation analysis results as sources of evidence for enhancing literature search.
